title: Thresholded WinCurve Insights — model-stability vs quality tradeoffs
content:
Summary:
This note captures the results and operational interpretation of the 'thresholded win-curve' analysis we ran during the November sprint. The goal: compare three candidate variants for the streaming-text endpoint and understand how small calibration/quantization changes move win rates across utility thresholds, and where stability (consistency across repeated prompts) becomes the dominant selection factor.

Key models evaluated (short names used in tables below):
- rw-1.9-base (float16 baseline, latest tokenizer)
- rw-2.0-quant-int8 (post-training quant, int8 kernels)
- rw-2.0-quant-q4f (mixed 4-bit profile, aggressive size reduction)

Datasets / prompt-sets used:
- product-support-50k: real user support prompts sampled (anonymized), skewed toward longer context (median 98 tokens).
- assistant-fewshot-5k: curated assistant-style prompts with multi-turn.
- webqa-2k: short factual Q/A to stress precision.

Methodology highlights (repro steps):
1) For each prompt we run 5 seeds (different sampling RNG) per model to estimate response variance and median utility.
2) Utility is a composite score: 0–100 from the automated rubric (answer correctness 60%, hallucination penalty 20%, brevity/format 20%) — calibrated against a 400-example human eval set.
3) Thresholded win-curve: for utility thresholds t in {40,50,60,70,80}, compute P(model A wins | utility_A >= t or utility_B >= t) and also joint-stability: fraction of prompts where winner is consistent across seeds.
4) Win/loss ties are handled by average utility; ties counted as 0.5 win.

Top-level findings (short):
- At low utility thresholds (t <= 50) rw-2.0-quant-int8 has the highest raw win-rate (overall win-rate vs rw-1.9-base = +6.4%). This is largely due to slightly more aggressive generation diversity that hits the low-quality-but-relevant bucket more often.
- At mid thresholds (t=60–70) win rates converge; rw-1.9-base and rw-2.0-quant-int8 trade places depending on prompt length.
- At high thresholds (t >= 80) rw-1.9-base clearly dominates rw-2.0-quant-q4f (win-rate delta +9.8%), while rw-2.0-quant-int8 lags by ~3–4% compared to base.
- Stability (seed-wise agreement) is best for rw-1.9-base (median agreement 87%), rw-2.0-quant-int8 is 75%, rw-2.0-quant-q4f is 62%. Stability correlates strongly with high-threshold wins (r=0.72).

Representative thresholded-win numbers (aggregated across all prompts):
- t=50: rw-2.0-quant-int8 win-rate 0.512, rw-1.9-base 0.449, rw-2.0-quant-q4f 0.420
- t=60: rw-1.9-base 0.489, rw-2.0-quant-int8 0.476, rw-2.0-quant-q4f 0.402
- t=80: rw-1.9-base 0.561, rw-2.0-quant-int8 0.531, rw-2.0-quant-q4f 0.463
(Notes: numbers are aggregated probabilities across pairwise comparisons normalized to sum=1 for readability)

Win/Loss patterns by prompt length bucket:
- Short (<32 tokens): quantized variants (int8 and q4f) close the gap; int8 slightly favored due to faster sampling leading to better early-token completions.
- Mid (32-128 tokens): parity zone — rw-1.9-base favored on complex reasoning prompts, int8 favored on instruction-following where brevity helps.
- Long (>128 tokens): rw-1.9-base advantage increases (consistency + reduced drift). q4f shows clear degradation in multi-step tasks (drop in correctness signals).

Operational interpretation and risks:
- If product SLOs prioritize cost reductions and can accept small regressions on the 80+ utility tail, rw-2.0-quant-int8 is attractive: ~22% lower GPU memory footprint, 1.6x effective throughput on our deduped workload.
- If we prioritize end-user experience for high-quality completions (help center, legal summarization), rw-1.9-base remains the safer choice because stability maps to perceived quality.
- q4f (rw-2.0-quant-q4f) currently fails regressions for multi-step assistant tasks and should not be onboarded for the streaming endpoint without further tuning.

Decision recommendation (for this sprint):
- Default rollout: keep rw-1.9-base as default for hosted streaming endpoints for now.
- Canary experiment: deploy rw-2.0-quant-int8 behind a tiered routing policy (10% traffic, high-variance allowed) targeted to short-mid prompts. Collect live signal for 2 weeks focusing on: degraded human-ratings >75th percentile, error spike detection, and latency-tail regressions.
- Blocker: do not promote q4f variants to production until we have an improved calibration pass (see next steps).

Suggested eval / follow-up work (practical next steps):
- Run a targeted calibration job for rw-2.0-quant-int8 focusing on temperature/top-p schedules that maximize high-threshold stability (we saw stability improvements of up to +6% with temperature tuning in early experiments).
- Add a deterministic sampling pilot (greedy or beam) for a subset of customer-critical flows to isolate sampling variance effects.
- Expand human eval set to 1k multi-step examples from long-context support cases — current 400 sample set underweights long-context failure modes.
- Investigate kernel-level numeric drift for q4f in our runtime (open ticket: RW-491).

Unresolved questions / notes to triage in next sync:
- Is the current automated utility rubric over-penalizing brevity? Some support prompts that are concise and correct score lower because format reward is small. Need a quick manual review.
- Live traffic covariate shift: will user prompt-length distribution in production differ materially from our sampled set (product-support-50k)? Plan a 48-hour production sniff to verify.

Appendix (quick reproducibility pointers):
- Eval harness: github.com/redwood-inference/model-evals commit 8f2b3d7 (PR #312) contains the exact scripts and seed lists.
- Key metrics endpoint: internal dashboard "thresholded-wincurves" (console -> product_evals -> wincurve).
- Jira/Linear tickets: RW-491 (q4f numeric drift), RW-503 (canary observability hooks).

Short lived TODOs (owner in parens):
- Turn on canary routing for int8 (Samir) — target date 2025-11-18.
- Calibration run for int8 (Evelyn) — target date 2025-11-25.
- Expand long-context human eval (Marco) — target date 2025-12-05.

If you want a quick view: I can export the per-prompt win/loss CSV (5M rows) to the shared bucket; otherwise I included a small sampled CSV in the PR (#312) for manual inspection.

Notes to reviewers: focus on the stability sections and the 'high-threshold' numbers — those are the most product-visible. If you disagree with the decision framing (cost-first vs quality-first), call it out explicitly in the PR review so we can attach a short rationale for the routing policy.

-- Ava
